text:
No. At six people, microservices mostly add cost: network boundaries, distributed debugging, per-service deploy pipelines, data consistency problems, and on-call surface area. The benefits (independent team scaling and deploys) only pay off when coordination between teams is the bottleneck, and with six engineers it isn't.

What would change this: a specific component with a genuinely different scaling profile (e.g., heavy video processing or ML inference), a hard isolation or compliance requirement, or a monolith deploy/test cycle that has become unmanageably slow despite fixes. Even then, extract that one piece as a single service rather than migrating wholesale.

Better investments now: enforce module boundaries inside the monolith (Packwerk or Rails engines), keep background work in Sidekiq or similar, and fix slow tests and deploys directly. Those preserve the option to extract later, and clean boundaries are what make extraction cheap.

The strongest case for splitting is if your pain is actually something else, such as a tangled codebase where people block each other. Microservices don't fix that; they relocate it across a network. If you tell me the specific pain driving the question, I can say whether any of it needs a service boundary.
